1.q: אֵ֭יךְ תֹּאמְר֣וּ לְ⁠נַפְשִׁ֑⁠י נודו הַרְ⁠כֶ֥ם צִפּֽוֹר׃ כִּ֤י הִנֵּ֪ה הָ⁠רְשָׁעִ֡ים יִדְרְכ֬וּ⁠ן קֶ֗שֶׁת כּוֹנְנ֣וּ חִצָּ֣⁠ם עַל־יֶ֑תֶר לִ⁠יר֥וֹת בְּמוֹ־אֹ֝֗פֶל לְ⁠יִשְׁרֵי־לֵֽב׃ כִּ֣י הַ֭⁠שָּׁתוֹת יֵֽהָרֵס֑וּ⁠ן צַ֝דִּ֗יק מַה־פָּעָֽל
1.note: Many Bible scholars think that David’s quote of his advisors begins with the words **Flutter like a bird to your mountain** and ends at the end of verse three. Some Bible scholars think that **Flutter like a bird to your mountain** are the only words of his advisors that David is quoting and that verses 2–3 are his own words. The ULT and UST follow option one. If a translation exists in your region that follows option two, you may wish to follow that option.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a physical place of safety or shelter. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I trust in Yahweh to keep me safe] or [I depend on Yahweh to protect me]

David is using the question form to challenge what people are telling him. His question continues from this verse to the end of verse 3. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not say to my soul]

The psalmist is using **my soul** to represent all of himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [can you say to me]

Here the speaker’s advisors are speaking of him as if he were actually a **bird** that should fly away to safety in the mountains. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Run away and hide in the mountains] or [Escape to safety in the mountains]

2.note: The psalmist is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully] or [Pay attention to this]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in 1:1. Alternate translation: [wicked men]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and motives exist. The phrase **upright of heart** describes people whose thoughts and motives are morally straight and righteous. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at those who think and act righteously] or [at those who live with pure motives]

3.note: The speaker is using the question form to emphasize that the **righteous** cannot do anything if the foundations of society are destroyed. If your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement. [If the foundations are destroyed, the righteous can do nothing.] or [If the foundations are destroyed, there is nothing the righteous can do.]

This question is the end of what people are saying to David, which he uses the question form in verses 1–3 to challenge. If you chose in verse 1 to represent his challenge as a statement or exclamation, end this with a period or exclamation point.

Here the psalmist is speaking as if the principles of justice and morality were actually **foundations** of a building. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the principles of justice and morality are destroyed] or [the moral order has broken down]
See how you translated the phrase **the righteous** in 1:5. Alternate translation: [righteous people]

4.q: יְהוָ֤ה ׀ בְּֽ⁠הֵ֘יכַ֤ל קָדְשׁ֗⁠וֹ יְהוָה֮ בַּ⁠שָּׁמַ֪יִם כִּ֫סְא֥⁠וֹ
4.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of God’s presence in heaven as if he were actually in a **temple** and as if **the heavens** were a place with a **throne**. You could translate the words literally or your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is present in his holy sanctuary and rules as king from heaven]

4.q: יְהוָ֤ה ׀ בְּֽ⁠הֵ֘יכַ֤ל קָדְשׁ֗⁠וֹ יְהוָה֮ בַּ⁠שָּׁמַ֪יִם כִּ֫סְא֥⁠וֹ
4.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation, if possible. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is in his holy temple; yes, Yahweh is in the heavens, his throne] or [Yahweh is in his holy temple; indeed, Yahweh is in the heavens, his throne]

The psalmist is not distinguishing this **throne** from another throne that is not in heaven. The psalmist is showing God’s greatness compared to human rulers who rule from a throne on earth, by adding that **the heavens** are the place of God’s **throne** (where he rules from). Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is in the heavens, they are his throne] or [Yahweh’s throne is in the heavens]
Here, God’s **throne** represents his “rule.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh rules from the heavens]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [His eyes see the sons of men] or [His eyes see everything that people do]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation, if possible. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [His eyes see, yes, his eyelids test] or [His eyes see, indeed, his eyelids test]

Here, **eyes** and **eyelids** represent God’s ability to see and evaluate everything people do. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [He sees, he tests]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “all human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the children of mankind] or [every human being]

5.note: See how you translated the phrase **the righteous** in 1:5. Alternate translation: [righteous people]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in 1:1. Alternate translation: [wicked men]

The psalmist is using **soul** to represent all of Yahweh in the act of hating. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he hates]

6.note: See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in 1:1. Alternate translation: [wicked men]

6.q: אֵ֣שׁ וְ֭⁠גָפְרִית וְ⁠ר֥וּחַ זִלְעָפ֗וֹת מְנָ֣ת כּוֹסָֽ⁠ם
6.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [may fire and brimstone and a scorching wind be the portion of their cup]

The phrase **fire and brimstone and a scorching wind** could refer to: (1) an actual physical judgment of fire and brimstone such as what happened to the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah in Genesis 19:24–25 (2) a judgment of some type, but not necessarily with fire and brimstone and a scorching wind. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language.

Here the psalmist is speaking as if **the portion of their cup** is what the wicked would receive as their share, like a drink that had been poured into their cup. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh will give them as their punishment]

7.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he loves those who do righteous things] or [he loves when people do what is righteous]

The psalmist is using the adjective **upright** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [upright people] or [those who do what is right]

David is using Yahweh’s **face** to represent Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will see him]
